beats.care: When RBI hikes rates or hints at future moves, it's using ideas like these. They shape your loan EMIs and how fast prices rise.
beats.what: Robert Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia won the 2026 economics Nobel, announced in Stockholm on Monday.
beats.why: Their models explain how households and businesses react to expected income, prices and interest rates. Central banks use them to fight inflation and slumps.

cards.body: In 1982, Hall and Fredric Mishkin found about 80% of households plan spending around expected future income; the rest live hand to mouth, spending what they earn now. Woodford's 2003 'New Keynesian' model is one many central banks rely on.
It's when a central bank says publicly what it plans to do next. If people believe it, they adjust prices and spending early, so the policy works faster.
cards.title: what is forward guidance?

cards.body: The new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, says forward guidance has gone too far and wants the Fed to talk less about its thinking.

cards.q: Should RBI tell us its next move in advance?

opts: Expectations about the future shape what people do today
cards.q: What big idea links the two winners?
cards.why: Both showed that people and firms act on what they expect next, which is why central banks speak so carefully.

hook: Why does RBI *explain* its moves? This year's economics Nobel is why

learn.t: Woodford showed that what people expect about future interest rates shapes prices today, which is why central banks explain their plans.
